Adaptations of Literature

How the written word is rewritten for the screen — and what gets kept, cut, and reimagined along the way.

Course description

This course studies how the written word is adapted to the screen, along with the cultural and historical dimensions of that process. Adaptation is treated as a form of representation and rewriting — especially cinematic adaptations of significant events in history and their impact on viewers today. The course challenges the conventional hierarchy that privileges literature over film, pairing classic texts with contemporary works more relevant to students' present-day world, and tracing intertextuality across page, stage, and screen.

Students are literature-focused, but leaning into film — this course sits at that intersection, contributing perspective on how written content becomes adaptable for stage or screen.

Course objectives

After successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

01

Understand and demonstrate knowledge of major adaptation theories, and engage with them critically.

02

Analyze how literary texts are reworked for visual media, with particular attention to representation and form.

03

Explore intertextuality between adaptations and their original source material — including how films present different frames of representation, or misrepresentation.

04

Examine how historical context, period, and cultural trends shape the translation of literature into film — and how the industry responds to the belief that literature is inherently "better" than film.

Sixteen weeks, ten units

Condensed from the week-by-week schedule.

WEEK 1

Foundations

What is an adaptation? What is intertextuality? Introduced through Corrigan's Film and Literature.

WEEKS 2–3

Pride & Prejudice

Austen's novel against the 2005 film — compare and contrast discussion.

WEEKS 4–5

The Outsiders — stage & screen

Hinton's novel, the 1983 film, and clips from the 2024 Broadway production.

WEEK 6

Fidelity theory & final project kickoff

Response paper due; students begin experimenting with the AI Visual Interactive Explorer.

WEEKS 7–8

Shakespeare in adaptation

Excerpts from four plays; discussion of which film versions stay closest to the text.

WEEKS 9–10

The Great Gatsby

Fitzgerald's novel, the 2013 film, and the Broadway production.

WEEK 11

Digital Storyline draft

First outline of each student's own adaptation, built with the AI Digital Storyline and Study Guide tools.

WEEKS 12–13

Wuthering Heights

Imagery and aesthetics across the 1939 and 2026 film versions.

WEEKS 14–15

The Odyssey

Language and translation, from Fagles' text to the 2026 film.

WEEK 16

Final project

Completed Digital Storyline and 2,000-word reflective essay due.

"AI is an assistant to your own thoughts, not a replacement for your voice."

Two agentic tools are built into the course: a Study Guide app for textual analysis and critical prompting, and a Digital Storyline template that maps each student's final project outline. Assignments that require AI tools are always specified — otherwise, students are encouraged to reach for their own thought process first. AI-generated text can never be claimed as original authorship, and every output must be verified before use.

03 · Signature Assignment

The Digital Storyline

An AI-driven structure that guides students as they plan their adaptation outline for the final project — an interactive narrative tool, but for the author's own choices rather than the reader's.

Using their chosen source material, students work through a guided framework of every element that makes an adaptation succeed — changing the story to fit a new vision while staying aware of what remains from the original. The tool also helps establish the cultural significance, historical context, and representation of the source story, and how each will carry into the new version.

Seven elements of the storyline

Each element maps to a theory of adaptation or a building block of storytelling.

01

Point of View

Whose lens the story is told through — frames how the audience experiences events.

02

Characters

Who drives the narrative — the protagonist the audience follows.

03

Motivation

What the character wants, and the stakes if they fail.

04

Emotional Connection

The feelings the story evokes, and why the audience cares.

05

Cultural / Historical Connection

Context that grounds the story and ties it to a larger moment.

06

Soundtrack

Music that sets the mood, and reinforces pacing and tone.

07

Symbolism

Objects or images with meaning that deepen the message.

Seven elements that turn a sequence of facts into a story worth watching.

Context for delivery

By the time students reach the Digital Storyline, they've already gathered research through the Study Guide app's "Planning My Adaptation" prompts — perspective, tone, fidelity — and pulled visual ideas from the Visual Interactive Explorer, which surfaces design choices from their source material's book covers. Both feed directly into the storyline outline.

04 · Teaching Statement

On teaching adaptation, with AI as a supplement

Natalie Romeo

I believe students learn best when offered multimodal pathways to engage with, process, and articulate information. I believe it necessary to support students with options that inspire different ways of interpreting content — especially in our ever-evolving, technologically advancing classrooms. An emphasis on a digitally enhanced curriculum provides students with diverse methods of learning while encouraging digital literacy and critical thinking. My pedagogical approach is rooted in the principles of Universal Design for Learning, specifically implementing multiple means of representation, action, and expression. I encourage treating digital humanities tools as an interpretive framework for learning because it is crucial in this increasingly algorithmic culture.

Finding a balance of integrating artificial intelligence into the classroom while maintaining learning equality is important. Rather than viewing generative tools as either a threat to traditional scholarship or a total replacement for original thought, I utilize AI as a supplemental engine for ideation, comparative analysis, and iterative critique. However, the discrepancy appears when students reach for AI to "think" for them or allow it to passively replace their own voice. At times, this creates a dilemma for teachers who have to put limitations in place instead of embracing all of the advantages it allows. Alternatively, when framed through a digital humanities lens, technology becomes an accessory to the lesson and can be perceived as an enhancement to learning rather than a crutch.

AI usage should be considered in relation to the necessities of the workflow — and should always be supplemental to thought, not a replacement.

By specifically structuring assignments around the mechanics and conditions of these tools, I guide students to interrogate how knowledge is constructed. An example of this is a project I developed for LIT4114 Adaptations of Literature. The signature project asks students to create an outline of a new adaptation from a piece of literature, using AI-driven tools to brainstorm ideas and further develop concepts. The tools are provided as a guide for research purposes and to help students compile information for the final project — a valuable influence of AI. However, maintaining awareness of action and expression regarding AI usage is important to uphold. Recognizing that student comfort levels with technology vary, I also designed flexible assignment parameters: students always retain the freedom to use traditional qualitative methods instead.

For a hiring committee seeking to emerge from traditional methods, this interdisciplinary approach is rooted in digital humanities because it encourages multidimensional learning. With this in mind, I aim to prepare and affiliate students to work alongside a technologically advancing world — changing the narrative around artificial intelligence and investigating new ways of engaging with it that enhance teaching practices. While I would never intend to abandon departmental traditions, my digital humanities credentials have provided me with the philosophy of merging literary pedagogy with expanding technology.

Planning your own adaptation

Ten guided questions shape the creative decisions behind each student's Digital Storyline.

🎭
Medium & FormWhat medium are you adapting into, and how does that change the way the story is told?
✂️
What you'll cutWhich characters or subplots will you remove — and why are they less essential in your version?
➕
What you'll addWhat new elements will you introduce that weren't in the original?
🌍
Setting & TimeWill you change the time period or setting? How does that shift the meaning?
🗣️
Voice & PerspectiveWill you change the narrator or point of view? Whose voice will dominate?
💡
Central ThemeWhich theme will you amplify, and which will you downplay or reframe?
🎨
Tone & StyleHow will the tone differ — darker, lighter, more ironic, more sincere?
👥
CharactersWill any characters be merged, split, or recast? What does that change?
⚖️
FidelityHow faithful will you be to the source — and where do you deliberately diverge?
👁️
AudienceWho is your target audience, and how does that shape your choices?
